speechtext: Order, please. It is the practice in the House, and I note the previous speaker also fell into the same habit, of referring to hon. members by their constituencies or ministers by their functions, not by personal names.

The other colleague who was so invaluable in her assistance to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General (Mr. Chretien) was the minister of state responsible for the status of women. The result that was achieved by these efforts has been welcomed by all members of the House. The Minister of Justice deserves our most heartfelt congratulations for this

November 24, 1981
The Constitution
latest effort on his part as well as for the leading role he played in the initial agreement with the nine provinces.
The Minister of Justice and Attorney General obviously subscribes to the axiom that politics is the art of the possible and he possesses the fairness, the flexibility, the give and take and the openness which are the basic ground rules for achieving political objectives in a democratic society. As an example of effective politics, I hope it would both impress and influence some of our other ministers, Mr. Speaker.

I should now like to broach subjects of concern to some of my francophone and anglophone constituents. The francophones are concerned with the conflict that opposes Quebec and Ottawa with regard to the three points on which they failed to agree. Concerning the right to mobility and to gain livelihood, the Government of Canada proposes to guarantee, and 1 quote:
6. (1) Every citizen of Canada has the right to enter, remain in and leave Canada.
(2) Every citizen of Canada and every person who has the status of a permanent resident of Canada has the right
(a)	to move to and take up residence in any province; and
(b)	to pursue the gaining of a livelihood in any province.
Those rights, Mr. Speaker, would prevent the provinces from imposing unfair restrictions to the hiring of workers from Quebec or Newfoundland. Yet, this section offers some protection when unemployment is particularly severe. The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) offered to add special terms in order to meet the objections of the Quebec government. In view of the provisions of Bill 101 concerning the working language, the danger of a massive migration of workers from the other provinces to Quebec is minimal.
Section 6 will protect mostly Quebecers. As for Section 23, which recognizes for the first time the right of every francophone in the country to education in his mother tongue, let us keep in mind Mr. Speaker, that our society is becoming increasingly mobile. Enormous energy projects will cause temporary movements of population throughout the country. Quebecers will now be able to move with their whole family and be assured that their children may pursue their education in French. As for the objections of Quebec to the Canadian proposal, it should be noted that Mr. Levesque himself proposed a reciprocal agreement on education in both official languages in St. Andrew's two or three years ago. The third point in dispute between Quebec and Ottawa concerns the lack of compensation for a province which decides to opt out of an amendment affecting its powers. The resolution now before the House make an additional concession to Quebec in Section 39.
Section 39 reads as follows:
39. Where an amendment is made under subsection 37(1) that transfers provincial legislative powers relating to education or other cultural matters from provincial legislatures to Parliament, Canada shall provide reasonable compensation to any province to which the amendment does not apply.
Quebec will therefore have a veto in matters of education and culture.
Another element of this resolution should be of interest to all Quebecers. I am referring to Section 35:
Equalization and regional disparities
The equalization system is of great benefit to all Canadians since it promotes equal opportunities throughout the country, but it is of special benefit to the provinces receiving money, including Quebec. Section 35 of the charter guarantees this principle of sharing and makes it a cornerstone of our Confederation.
What does equalization mean for Quebecers? It means that the wealth produced by the natural resources of western Canada will be shared with Quebecers and maritimers. When the west is prosperous, all Canadians benefit from new job opportunities, economic spin-offs for industry and the sharing of tax revenues guaranteed by equalization.
The concerns of my English-speaking fellow Quebecers relate particularly to the optional applicability of the maternal language clause, Section 23(l)(a). They are asking why the maternal language clause is being applied in the other nine provinces but not in Quebec. Apart from the political arguments, with which I will deal in a moment, the practical argument which the government employs is that the absence of French schooling facilities in most parts of English Canada means that many French Canadian families would be ineligible under the other subsections of Section 23 to send their children to French schools. They would not have benefited from French schooling facilities since none exist. That handicap does not affect the English-speaking inhabitants of Quebec who have long had excellent school facilities provided by the government of Quebec and supported by all taxpayers of Quebec.
The number of people affected by the non-applicability of Section 23(1 )(a) is fairly small. Perhaps we are talking about 2,000 to 3,000 naturalized Canadian citizens, couples who came to Quebec from elsewhere in Canada after the passage of Bill 101. They had not started families or did not have children in school prior to moving to Quebec. They are families with at least one parent whose maternal language is English. Bill 101 allows all inhabitants of Quebec whose maternal language is English, domiciled there at the time of the passage of the bill, to send their children to English language schools. We are faced with a situation where admittedly the 2,000 to 3,000- and I do not know if my figures are accurate-couples who moved to Quebec since Bill 101 from other parts of Canada will not have rights which are available to other Canadians anywhere else in the country. We are also talking about another group of a few thousand or more naturalized Canadians who came to Quebec since the passage of Bill 101 from outside Canada and whose mother tongue is English. In this case the people who came knew what they were facing when
November 24, 1981

they came; the bill had been passed, and they are not stuck with a situation which was thrust upon them after the fact.
The reason I am quoting these statistics is to underline that the numbers are insignificant from a demographic viewpoint or from the viewpoint of a threat to Quebec's French majority.
There is a third group which is potentially affected by the section, that is the English language immigrant group that could be expected to total perhaps 2,000 to 4,000 per year over the next few years, if the statistics of the last several years hold accurate. This group is of particular importance. These people usually come from the United States or Great Britain because their skills are particularly in demand by sectors of the Quebec economy.
[ Translation]
Whether we like it or not, we in Canada suffer from a shortage of skilled workers in various fields, including geologists and geophysicists in western Canada as well as aerospace technicians in Quebec. The blame rests squarely on the federal and provincial governments as well as on industry. Nevertheless, if we fail to improve our technical training programs, Canada will continue to import those skilled workers from other countries. It is precisely those skilled technicians and their availability to develop Quebec's aerospace industry which will be affected by our lack of courage with respect to Section 23(1 )(a). Mr. Speaker, we are not talking about waves of English-speaking immigrants who will severely upset the demographic balance in Quebec but instead just a few thousand couples.

The statistics of the last decade demonstrate that Quebec's native English-speaking population, young people in particular, educated at the expense of Quebec taxpayers, has been moving westward to take advantage of greater opportunities in far larger numbers than they have been replaced by Englishspeaking immigrants. The English-speaking percentage of Quebec's population has been diminishing rapidly over the years. We are not talking about any threat to the French-language majority in Quebec. Even the Parti Quebecois now admits that the demographic views, which were a major factor behind the growth of the separatist movement, are no longer justified by statistics.
As I have already alluded, if the absence of the maternal language clause in Section 23(1 )(a) will be bad for Quebec's economy, in particular the aerospace industry, and if there is no demographic threat, why are we showing such lack of courage?
It is the political judgment of my colleagues in the House of Commons from Quebec, that imposing Section 23(l)(a), the maternal language clause now, would provide the Parti Quebecois separatists with a rallying cry, to the detriment of the acceptance of the entire package by the Quebec population. It is more important, they argue, to win the larger war against separatism than to jeopardize popular Quebec, as distinct from
The Constitution
the Quebec government, acceptance of the present constitutional package.
While I accept that argument, I frankly do not believe the battle for the minds and loyalties of Quebecers will be greatly affected by this issue. Wisdom dictates a quick, clearcut decision, rather than to leave it a festering cause of future discussion and perhaps controversy.
I believe that the Quebec public is far better informed and better able to judge the facts than they are given credit for by both federal and provincial politicians.
By leaving out Section 23(1 )(a) now and allowing Quebec to opt in later, we are, in effect, surrendering to the threat of Parti Quebecois demagoguery. I do not think we should succumb to that threat.
Quebec members are in a strong position to handle Parti Quebecois arguments regarding the application of Section 23(1 )(b) which allows Canadians who have received their education in English or French anywhere in Canada to pass on that right to English or French language education to their children. We can also handle the argument relating to Section 23(2) which allows the family of any child of a Canadian citizen who has started his education in English or French to continue the education of all the children of the family in that same language anywhere in Canada, because Mr. Levesque himself proposed such a formula based on reciprocity at a premier's conference in St. Andrews a few years ago.
Why not have Section 23(l)(a) as well or, I would urge the Prime Minister, at least have an exception to the non-applicability of Section 23(1 )(a) to allow Canadians who moved to Quebec since passage of Bill 101, the choice of language? Maternal English language immigrants who came to the country after that time were clearly aware what they were coming to as were Canadians who moved to Quebec. To me it seems that a distinction can and should be made in favour of Canadians, perhaps without families, who moved to Quebec for a year or two, then decided to stay and raise families, that they be allowed to make the choice that their English-speaking co-inhabitants of Quebec have under the existing Quebec law and should have as a result of the changes proposed in the Constitution. To do otherwise, I would argue, is not in keeping with the contents and spirit of the resolution we are debating tonight.
[ Translation]
A moment ago I expressed some reservations about the wisdom of excluding Quebec at this time from the application of section 23(1 )(a). Except for those reservations, I must say that I am proud to support the endeavour of the Prime Minister who has been anxious to guarantee full sovereignty for Canada. His initiative, his perseverance and, in recent weeks, his flexibility have now brought us to the point where patriating the Constitution has almost become a mere formality. It is indeed thanks to the courage and tenacity of the Right Hon. Prime Minister at each stage of the long process that his efforts will be successful. The charter will establish the principle of sharing our wealth among all regions of our country. It

will give Quebecers the assurance that they will enjoy the right to go anywhere without restrictions and to work in all parts of Canada.
The charter will guarantee that workers from Quebec will enjoy the right to have their children educated in French anywhere in Canada.

Canadians can be proud of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. They can be proud too that the political leadership of the country, both federal and provincial, has shown a new maturity in achieving consensus on the resolution we are debating tonight. The process has been a victory for the Canadian federal system, and all Canadians are the winners.

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I raised a very grave issue with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) which amounts to the invasion of Canadian jurisdiction by a foreign power in the absence of any appropriate Canadian citizenship legislation to protect the citizens from Czechoslovakia, in this case, from the blandishments and coercion of that country.
This is a very serious matter. The minister's response to my question indicated that he really did not have very much
knowledge of the issues involved at that time. In fairness, however, I suppose he has now been briefed.
In contrast, his colleague, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), who is more concerned with matters of security, in response to questions from my colleague, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), indicated that he was aware of the gravity of what has been going on. Since 1977 a very sincere and erudite columnist, Lubor Zink, has been bringing this particular matter to the attention of the Canadian people. Indeed, he has grilled the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about it and brought it to the attention of a former minister of external affairs, the Hon. Don Jamieson.
For anyone who is interested in dog dancing and evasiveness on the part of the Prime Minister on the very important issue on rights and sovereignty, Mr. Zink's column is most instructive, particularly now when the House is concerned with a Charter of Rights and Freedoms for our people.
Lest anyone be misled that this is only an academic problem, I want to refer to a current letter which illustrates the problem very well. It came from a Canadian citizen who asked for my advice, although he is not one of my constituents. He said that he and his family had escaped from Czechoslovakia soon after the Russian invasion in 1968, when he was a child. He is now a Canadian citizen and he is proud of it. He applied at the Czechoslovakian embassy to have his former citizenship formally revoked, and his application was finally approved.
Now, however, it appears that the Communists have raised a new demand. He is asked to pay $215 for the document which repudiates his former Czech citizenship. He is quite prepared to pay that amount provided the whole matter is not simply a Communist hoax designed to gain worthy currency. He asked whether he would really be free, with no strings attached, from his former association with the governing clique in Prague. He wondered, for example, whether he could visit Czechoslovakia in the future without fear of detention, arrest or disappearance. He wrote, "You have been helping Canadians of Czech origin for many years. Surely, you have some information regarding this policy of revoking citizenship for payment".
It was not to me that this letter was written but to one of my colleagues. What is my colleague to advise this Canadian citizen? Obviously, he cannot in all good conscience say that if this citizen goes down to the Czech embassy he will not, in fact, be grilled and will not be asked to fill in some very, very personal information, including information on all of his connections in the old country, his relatives, and what he has been doing ever since he got here. It would be very instructive for all hon. members to read the kind of questions that Czech emigres are forced to answer in order to deal with their people back in Czechoslovakia.
One cannot really attribute this kind of reprehensible behaviour to just one particular country. However, Czech-slovakia seems to be particularly good at it. However, other Iron Curtain countries are using this kind of tactic on their
November 24, 1981

citizens simply because Canada has not had the guts to do anything about this.
Our Citizenship Act was changed a few years ago. There are really no sanctions, and there is no encouragement to help those who are contemplating whether they should submit to what amounts to blackmail in order to make contact with their loved ones or go back to a country which still means something to them for traditional reasons. The Czechs are doing this in Canada and are applying pressure to Canadians who, in some cases, have sensitive positions and have in fact accepted Czech passports and travel back to Czechalovakia and, I believe, pose a security risk to our country.
In the same way the Czechs are doing this-and we are doing nothing about it-the Soviet Union is using these kinds of tactics on people in that country. Do not think for one moment that when people of Jewish persuasion want to leave the Soviet Union, they too must submit to this kind of blackmail paid by them or their relatives? They are not prepared to say, "Well, comrades, this goes on in Canada, you know. Czech people whose citizenship is still enforced by Czechoslovakia do not mind paying money for the privilege of going back to Czechoslovakia. They will take affirmations showing either loyalty or pledging to do nothing against the Czech socialist republic." It is a reprehensible situation. It is an insult to our country.
Lubor Zink summed up the situation very well in one of his colums in December of 1977 after bringing it to the attention of the then minister of external affairs and the Prime Minister. Concerning the false arguments with regard to the so-called dual nationality with which the govvernment cannot seem to come to grips, he said:
It would be very strange indeed if political refugees were to lose the protection they have as stateless persons who had been granted political asylum, the moment they become citizens of a host country.
That host country is us, ourselves, and we cannot protect them because we simply do not have the guts to do it. For example, we purchase a great deal of goods and services from Czechoslovakia. During the last seven or eight years, we have purchased approximately $324 million worth. We have sold them only $113 million worth. Has no one thought of using a little of our feeble economic leverage on Czechoslovakia, or are we just going to continue to submit to this kind of treatment?
It is not as if the security service is not aware of this, or the Solicitor General, or, surely by now, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan). This matter has been raised repeatedly. Hon. members must know that the Czech secret service is second only to the KGB itself in terms of its effectiveness and operations in Canada. Hon. members must know, as well, that any commercial dealings with this country by the Czechs or by the Soviet Union are simply a cover to obtain intelligence and to finance espionage against our country. When will we do something about this to protect our own citizens of Czech origin?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon.
Adjournment Debate
member for bringing this matter to the attention of the House again. Although it is ten o'clock and there are few people in the House, and few hon. members, I think it is important because Canada is one of the most respected democracies in the world. The opinion of this democracy is that what Cze-choslovokia is doing now is wrong. We hope that message is delivered to Czechoslovakia.
As my hon. friend has indicated, former Czech citizens who are now Canadian citizens are forced, in some instances, not all, to complete questionnaires, to be interviewed and to sign statements of allegiance to Czechoslovakia. This is really foreign to everything we think of as traditionally belonging to Canadian citizenship.
I think my hon. friend would admit, however, that Czechoslovakia is a Communist country and is sovereign in its own right, and short of sending gun boats we are restricted to economic discussions and human rights discussions on this side, in the forefront, and persuasion. That is what we are trying to do. There have been discussions as recently as November 5, 1981, with the Czechoslovakian national association at the official level. We have discussed it with the Czechoslovakian authorities on several occasions in the context of one-to-one discussions and in the context of the conference on security and co-operation in Europe.
The Czechoslovakian position is not satisfactory to Canada, and we have so indicated. We have made it clear that we will not be satisfied until these Canadian citizens, albeit of Czechoslovakian descent, are no further harassed while abroad. We feel that at a maximum all they need be required to have in Czechoslovakia is a Canadian passport and a Czechoslovakian visa.
In 1980 discussions were started on this issue at the consular level to obtain a consular agreement, and it is an item in the second phase of the consular discussions that will begin in the first half of 1982. As Bismarck once remarked when they showed him the motto of his house "no steps backward, but a few zigzags". That is probably the way Canada has had to go traditionally and will have to go in the future-many zigzags to the desired goal, and the desired goal is to free these Czechoslovakian-Canadian citizens-I do not like hyphenated citizenship-Canadian citizens from this yoke of oppression.

AIRPORTS-CONTRACT TO OPERATE DUTY FREE STORES AT TORONTO INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 10 I asked a question of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) about the allocation of the duty free stores at Toronto International Airport to a foreign company, despite the presence of several acceptable bids by Canadian companies. I believe that the giving of this contract to a foreign company was a mistake. We gave away the best duty free store location in Canada to a foreign company to the detriment of good Canadian firms. I believe we distorted the tendering procedures of the Ministry of Transport in the course of that,

November 24, 1981
Adjournment Debate
and I believe we gained nothing for Canadians that we could not already obtain for ourselves.
We have a fundamental obligation to foster Canadian enterprise. We must use the available resources of our government to bring the fruits of our own economic efforts under our own control and into the ownership of our own companies and people.
The short history of this duty free store location deserves to be told, partly because it shows how even in the government we can lose sight of this principle, partly to try to remedy the situation, and partly to bring us back on course in future situations like this.
The sequence of events is simple. In early 1979 the lease on this location had expired and we called for bids from new renters. There were two briefings for potential bidders, one on May 30, a verbal question and answer session, and one on June 12, a written supplementary session. In the normal situation that was prevailing at that time, the bids were to be received in August and the awards were to be made on November 1, 1979. The award was not made, however, until November 1, 1981. The reason is that Duty Free Shoppers of Honolulu and Hong Kong offered much higher sums for this location, much higher even that the estimates of the Ministry of Transport itself. As a result, the bidding process was greatly delayed and twisted about. Had the Ministry of Transport decided to give the contract directly to a Canadian company, that company would have received a contract right away, in 1979. Instead, the prior rules and principles, the prior regulations, were thrown out the window and there was a delay of two years.
I would like to quote from a Ministry of Transport document, the one I referred to just a moment ago. It is headed "Duty Free Briefing." It concerns a briefing which was held on May 30, 1979, at 1.30 p.m. at Toronto International Airport. The document is marked File No. 5156-381. On page 9 of that document there is the following question:
It is indicated in the tender specifications that conditional tenders will not be accepted. What happens in the situation where a tender is accepted and then is subsequently not approved by FIRA?
The question goes on a little further but the answer comes very clearly. It says:
Conditional tenders will NOT be considered.
To clarify the particular situation presented no tender will be accepted until it has received all necessary approvals. Hence any tender submitted subject to FIRA approval will be deemed to be a conditional tender and not considered.
However, Mr. Speaker, one of the bids from Duty Free Shoppers was so much higher that it was thrown out the window. On March 5, 1981, The Globe and Mail reported the reason for the long delay as follows:
Douglas Gerrie, acting director of airport marketing for the Ministry of Transport, said the long delay in reaching a decision is unusual. He said the reason was that "some of the highest bidders were out of country bidders and there had been no decision by FIRA with respect to certain aspects of their applications to operate in Canada."
Then, by November 10, the minister himself said in reply to my question-and I quote a portion of it:
When one of the foreign bidders appeared to be the winner a decision was made to get the case to FIRA. FIRA and my department developed a regime for duty-free shops.
In other words, as soon as the money was worth it we threw out the tendering and the prior regulations and we forgot about our own principles.
Now, when FIRA agreed to approve the right by Duty Free Shoppers to bid, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) said, and I quote from a FIRA press release of October 29:
-Mr. Gray noted that allowance of the 422694 proposal should result in a greater number of bidders for the airport concession and, if 422694 is successful in its bid, will bring to Canada the expertise of its affiliates in operating duty-free concessions-
What I would like to know, Mr. Speaker, is this. There were half a dozen Canadian companies bidding on that contract. Why do we need what the minister called "a greater number of bidders"? Every last one of them already deals with the Ministry of Transport. What expertise are they lacking? What extra ingredients do they bring? And when we look through the other concessions made by FIRA, the other undertakings made to FIRA, we find no additional benefit to Canada that this company brings that our own people were not able to give us already. Mr. Speaker, the final concern that I have comes from one of the undertakings made to FIRA itself-and I will conclude on this:
-to waive any right, which it-
That is, Duty Free Shoppers-
-might acquire through allowance under the FIR Act, to engage concurrently or subsequently in any related business in Canada, excepting the operation of other duty-free concessions, without prior approval under the FIR Act;
Not only have we allowed this company to come here, to the detriment of Canadian companies already operating, but we are also going to let this happen again in the future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-CONTRACT TO OPERATE DUTY FREE STORES AT TORONTO INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, Duty Free Shoppers Limited, an American firm, has been awarded the duty free concession at Toronto International Airport. The hon. member's main objection seems to be that the award was made to a foreign firm. The explanation is simply that the firm in question submitted by far the highest bid, and was willing to meet the conditions imposed by FIRA.
In this particular situation, the submission of bids by foreign firms required the development of new FIRA guidelines that could be used to evaluate the applications. The guidelines, as indicated by the minister in answer to the original question on November 10, stipulate a very high Canadian content.
It should be clear that the tender specifications did not preclude foreign firms from submitting bids. This question was in fact raised during the pre-tender briefing, in the context of whether a tender should be submitted "subject to" the approval of FIRA to ensure that the tenderer's security deposit be returned. It was clarified that tenders must be self-supporting and not subject to extraneous considerations. Sections 5 and 6
November 24, 1981

of the "terms and conditions" of the tender specifications clearly state that the lessee shall abide by all rules, regulations and bylaws of the federal, provincial or municipal governments. Consequently, if a tender was received subject to FIRA or any other approval, it would be rejected. In the end, no tenderer submitted an offer of this sort.
With respect to the costs incurred in the tendering process, it should be noted that the tenderer has the option of submitting security deposits in the form of certified cheques or Government of Canada bonds. Any company that is bidding in the millions of dollars is no doubt aware of the advantages and disadvantages of each option, and any tenderer will attempt to minimize his financial commitments. In fact, certain bidders for this concession did exchange their security deposits from certified cheques to bonds.
In conclusion, the government believes the contract was awarded fairly to the highest bidder. The conditions imposed by FIRA on this foreign company will ensure that Canadians will derive significant benefit from the contract.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to address the House on the subject of the Western Development Fund, the elusive dream mentioned in the October 28, 1980 budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and dealt with again on November 12 last. We find, however, that the transportation and resource fund of 1980 is the slush fund of 1981.
It is interesting to note the words of the Minister of Finance in his budget address of October 28, 1980. He said:
We have, therefore, allocated $4 billion to a Western Development Fund, of which we expect to spend $2 billion over the next three years... Specific development initiatives will be selected in consultation with the governments of the western provinces. They will be designed to address the major economic opportunities and constraints which will challenge the west during this decade. For example, the federal government is hopeful that through consultation with interested groups in the west, agreement can be reached on the modernization of the western grain handling and transportation system which is so vital to the growth and diversification of the prairie economy. We will also consider initiatives relating to industrial diversification and examine ways in which trade and industrial policies can better serve western development. To co-ordinate these efforts and to ensure early action, the Prime Minister has established a special group of ministers led by my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
What has become of that plan? The government has forgotten about it. No consultations have been held and no plans have been drawn up for the spending of these alleged billions of dollars.
Indeed, one wonders whether the government really knew what it had created. The simple fact is that nobody in the government had any intention of putting in place seed money for the development of industry in western Canada. They simply needed a fund they could dip their hands into when the pot was empty somewhere else.
Adjournment Debate
In the budget, we can plainly see how completely fraudulent this fund really is and what a cruel hoax has been perpetrated on the people of western Canada by this government. The fund has now been slashed to $1.5 billion from $4 billion, to be spread over five years instead of three. This year's allocations are at $148 million, down $202 million from this year's main estimates. In the budget, the government announced that the allocations are all intended to provide for improvements in the western transportation system. Now we find that $65 million will be used to assist Vancouver in the purchase of urban transit, light rapid transit. All that equipment comes from eastern Canada. So much for providing jobs and secondary industry and technology to the west.
What is even more disturbing is the use of the fund to funnel $81 million to Canadian farmers for payment for losses sustained because of the Soviet grain embargo. Canadian farmers have every right to their money. They must be compensated fairly for their loss. This government, however, is paying money to them from a fund declared to be for the economic development of the west. One should add that of the $81 million payment, $13 million goes to farmers in Ontario and Quebec. Both payments should have been paid out of the general treasury.
Grain embargo moneys out of a fund purportedly designed to place seed money in western Canada for industrial and transportation improvement and expansion is a complete betrayal of promises to western Canada. The use of the fund to buy an eastern transit system for Vancouver means no new industry and jobs for western Canadians. When the pot gets dry, western Canadians will pay again as we have in the past. The fund, created to turn some resource profits back to western Canada to build the west, is a fraud simply and purely, a mirage, a joke.
With the envelope system of expenditures having been accepted by the government, any moneys dedicated to the Western Development Fund will be used as a slush fund by cabinet to loosen up moneys in the envelope for other parts of the country. Thus, perversely, the so-called Western Development Fund is actually the antithesis of that. The government's actions are another in a long series of broken promises to the west. It is no wonder that the Liberal Party is the laughing stock of western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) packed a number of assertions into his questions to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) on November 16.
Among them was the assertion that the Western Development Fund has been and I quote "put out into Never Never Land until some time in the 1990s". It is true that the Minister of Finance's (Mr. MacEachen) budget has announced the government's decision on the first allocation of the fund, namely $1,355 billion for a major initiative on western transportation, and about $400 million for socioeconomic development of native peoples.

November 24, 1981
Adjournment Debate
The hon. member will understand why there has been a delay in the government's decisions about the western fund, as he is a former minister of energy, mines and resources. Contrary to the government's expectations at the time of last year's budget, the energy agreements with western producing provinces have just recently been concluded. As the principle for the creation of the fund, namely, the use of federal energy revenues to accomplish major projects within the federal government's mandate in the west-as this principle has guided the government's deliberations on this matter-the government had to await the outcome of the energy negotiations before making firm commitments and allocations.
The hon. member spoke of "Never Never Land", and "sometime in the 1980s" for the fund. Clearly, with the Minister of Finance's first allocations now announced, it is the hon. member who is living in some strange land. Maybe he is looking too far into the future for his own good.
I am particularly proud as a western member on this side of the House that the government's initial decisions on the western fund are intended for transportation-the single most critical and important physical infrastructure constraint upon western Canada's economic growth, and for native development.
All westerners know that, unfortunately, native peoples are at the present time the least well prepared to participate fully in the benefits that growth brings. Native development is thus the most critical and important human resources concern in western Canada. It is the government's promise that the western Development Fund will be used in part to assist native westerners in their quest for a better chance in the economic opportunity that the present boom brings.
